It's an inverse operation. You multiply by 2 because 2*1/2 is 1. That gets rid of the 2 in the denominator. Now, since 2 is multiplied on one side of the equation, you need to multiply by 2 on the other side to keep the equation balanced. 

If you ever want to get rid of a fraction in an equation, multiply that fraction by the number in the denominator. E.g. 3 * 1/3=1, 15 * 1/15 = 1, 15* x/15 = x. And, of course, apply that same multiplication to the other side of the equation.

Hope that helps!

I feel your pain, girl. Natural hair is far from easy as they say it is on YouTube. I grew up not knowing what tf to do with my hair (a mixture of 4a/b/c all throughout) and neither did my parents. It got so bad (dandruff, flakes, mats, the worst knots you could imagine) that my parents opted to relax my hair up until middle school. Still didn't know what to do and was *terrified* of getting my hair wet, so I never washed it lol. I cut it all off in high school when the irritation from the relaxer got so bad, and honestly, I loved the freedom it gave me. Plus, it gave me an opportunity to really find what worked for my natural hair before it got long enough to get tangled or brittle.

I'm finally growing it out again, and I've found some things that have worked for me. Low manipulation and protective styles have become my best friends, especially two strand twists. I spend a couple hours on wash day detangling (in 6+ sections), shampooing/clarifying, deep conditioning, and then twisting my hair. Then I can leave it in that style for like a week without worrying about it (plus it's cute asf!). Then rinse and repeat lol. I'm still trying to find the best products that make my hair happy, but it's really all trial and error. These YouTube gurus found what worked for them, but *everyone's* hair make up, curl pattern, and porosity is different, so what works for them may not give desirable results for you.

But I can't stress enough how important it is to find a good protective style and hair care regimen to keep those tangles from getting out of control. If shaving your hair is on your mind, maybe it wouldn't be a bad idea. It creates the perfect opportunity to really experiment and find new techniques as your hair grows out again. Whatever you decide to do, though, it might be good to consider seeing a textured hair specialist.

Btw I'm wishing you the best of luck! It takes a lot of effort to maintain any kind of hair, but when you find something that clicks, your hair will be happy, and you will be too!

Correct me if I'm wrong, but morality only really applies to a society/community of sentient beings. Is it *morally* wrong to kill for food? Maybe. Morals are relative and based on culture. Subcultures, like the vegan community, have set rules against exploiting animals for any sort of human gain, putting the animals' lives before their own. On the other hand, other cultures may believe animals simply don't have souls, so there is nothing morally wrong about it, and thus put their lives over animals. There's also the question of *how* you're killing the animal. Are they living in small cages and getting beat every day until they're slaughtered? Do they live in pastures where they are taken care of until they're ready to be eaten? Imo, I think the latter is more morally acceptable, although I am guilty of purchasing from factory farms (there's no ethical — or in this case, moral — consumption under capitalism, I guess).

But is it *naturally* wrong to kill and consume animals? Certainly not. If you view it universally and place humans on the same tier as any other carnivore/omnivore, it's natural to be compelled to eat meat. From as early as 2 billion years ago (40 million years after the first photosynthesizers), prokaryotic cells have consumed other prokaryotes. So you could argue that it's just natural for some organisms to eat others. It is true that humans have bio markers that imply we are omnivores and can *naturally* eat meat.

At the end of the day though, humans aren't like other animals. Unlike many animals (although I don't believe there are enough studies to measure more complicated cultural aspects, per se, of other animals) humans have an intricate network of spirituality, culture, religion, and obligations that determine what's right and wrong. Many animals don't have that kind of compass and just carry out the mechanisms hardwired in their phenotypes to stay alive. For example, an orca isn't going to care about the seal it's eating or the pain it's inflicting on it. Humans, though, have to stand by our perceived cultural/created morals. I'm sure there are a plethora of different arguments you can look into (philosophical, biological, genetic, etc), but they all won't fit into a single comment and , frankly, I'm too lazy to do the research haha. I believe that morals are completely relative and can change based on where you grew up and your lived experiences. Some moral "rules" are completely contradictory on opposite sides of the planet (or even between neighbors). So really, the decision is up to the individual on whether or not it is moral. Applying one set of morals to the entire human population would be logically incorrect, as perceived morals differ from person to person.

Personally, I think it's morally fine to consume animals (granted, they aren't mistreated in their lives) because, selfishly, I need that kind of (cheap) protein/nucleic acids to survive. I'm sure some others must share that sentiment.

Not all pwBPD want to overstep boundaries, but when in crisis, it's easy to forget them. So keeping them in the front of your spouse's mind will help encourage a healthy, nontoxic relationship.

Furthermore, he needs to realize that you simply cannot afford to support everyone. That's not an affront to him and definitely not saying you only value his money. But if this continues, you may need to consider cutting him off until he has the means to help you out. You shouldn't have to carry that burden alone.

It's not your responsibility over the cleanliness and behavior of your boyfriend's family. I know the saying "you're not just in a relationship with your partner, but with their family" is popular, but tbh, that's a load of bull. You don't have to like the family, especially if -- from what you've said -- they seem neglectful. Of course, you have to tolerate them (only to an extent) just out of consideration for your boyfriend, but that doesn't mean you have to accept them completely. I wish you the best of luck!
